roc.s: Each point on a ROC curve is a threshold: true positive rate against false positive rate. The diagonal is random guessing (AUC 0.5), and the closer to the top-left corner, the better. On rare positives, the precision-recall curve (right) is more telling, because its baseline is the positive rate, not 0.5.

confusion.s: Rows are what is true, columns what the model predicted. Precision = TP / (TP + FP) looks down the 'predicted positive' column. Recall = TP / (TP + FN) looks along the 'actually positive' row.

biasvar.s: Training error keeps falling as the model gets more flexible, while validation error turns upward once it starts fitting noise. The best model sits near the validation minimum. Too simple means high bias; too flexible means high variance.

gd.s: Each step moves against the gradient, scaled by the learning rate. Small rates converge smoothly but slowly. Rates that are too large jump across the valley and can diverge.

kmeans.s: The algorithm alternates two steps: assign each point to its nearest centroid, then move each centroid (+) to the mean of its points. It stops when assignments stop changing, and it needs k chosen in advance.

normal.s: A symmetric bell fully described by its mean and standard deviation. About 68% of values lie within one standard deviation, 95% within two. The central limit theorem says sample means tend to this shape even when the data does not.

pvalue.s: If the null hypothesis were true, the p-value is the chance of seeing a result at least this extreme: the shaded tail. It is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true.

acf.s: A stationary series has an autocorrelation that drops to near zero quickly (orange). Slow decay (blue) suggests a trend or a unit root, so difference the series before modelling.

pid.s: The controller acts on the error between setpoint and measurement. P reacts to the present error, I accumulates past error to remove steady offset, D reacts to the rate of change to damp overshoot. Integral windup occurs when I keeps growing while the output is saturated.

kalman.s: Each step predicts the state with the model, then corrects it with the measurement, weighted by the Kalman gain. The gain is high when the sensor is trusted more than the model, and low when the model is trusted more.

droop.s: A droop curve sets power as a function of frequency: below nominal the battery injects power, above it absorbs. The slope is the droop percentage, and the flat deadband avoids reacting to small noise.

ocv.s: NMC voltage rises steadily with charge, so voltage tells you the SOC. LFP is flat across most of the range, so a small voltage error means a large SOC error. That is why LFP needs Coulomb counting and filters.

thevenin.s: A cell is modelled as an ideal source (OCV) in series with R0 for the instant voltage step and an R1‖C1 pair for the slower relaxation. Terminal voltage = OCV − I·R0 − the RC pair voltage.

vcc.s: Refrigerant is compressed to a hot high-pressure gas, condenses and rejects heat, is throttled through the expansion valve to low pressure and temperature, then evaporates absorbing heat from the chilled-water loop. The compressor does the work.

three.s: Three sine waves are offset by 120°. Their sum is zero at every instant, so the delivered power is smooth and the neutral carries almost nothing when balanced. Line-to-line voltage is √3 times phase voltage.

ptri.s: Real power P and reactive power Q are at right angles, and apparent power S is the hypotenuse: S² = P² + Q². Power factor = P / S = cos φ. Reducing Q with a capacitor or inverter lowers the current for the same real power.
ptri.svg: <line class="l2" x1="60" y1="190" x2="300" y2="190"/><line class="l3" x1="300" y1="190" x2="300" y2="70"/><line class="ln" x1="60" y1="190" x2="300" y2="70"/><text x="180" y="212" text-anchor="middle" class="">P (kW) real</text><text x="335" y="135" text-anchor="middle" class="">Q (kvar)</text><text x="150" y="120" text-anchor="middle" class="">S (kVA) apparent</text><path class="ax" d="M100,190 a40,40 0 0,0 -6,-14"/><text x="122" y="182" text-anchor="middle" class="sm">φ</text>

pq.s: The converter's current limit makes a circle: P² + Q² ≤ S². At full active power there is no room for reactive power, and with less P it can supply more Q. Left and right sides are charging and discharging.
pq.svg: <line class="ax" x1="45" y1="130" x2="385" y2="130"/><line class="ax" x1="45" y1="130" x2="45" y2="20"/><path d="M385,130 l-7,-4 v8z M45,20 l-4,7 h8z" fill="#8794ab"/><text x="215.0" y="160" text-anchor="middle" class="">Real power P →</text><line class="ax" x1="215" y1="25" x2="215" y2="235"/><path class="ln" d="M80,130 A135,105 0 0,1 350,130"/><path class="ln" d="M80,130 A135,105 0 0,0 350,130"/><text x="215" y="18" text-anchor="middle" class="sm">+Q (inject)</text><text x="215" y="248" text-anchor="middle" class="sm">−Q (absorb)</text><text x="280" y="70" text-anchor="middle" class="">S limit: P² + Q² ≤ S²</text>

hbridge.s: Two switches alternate to connect the output to +Vdc or −Vdc. A dead time with both off prevents shoot-through (a short across the DC link). Filtering the switched output gives a sine; three legs make a three-phase inverter.

duck.s: Solar pushes net load (demand minus solar) down at midday, then it climbs steeply as the sun sets and demand peaks. Batteries charge in the belly and discharge on the ramp.

merit.s: Plants are dispatched from cheapest to most expensive until demand is met. The last plant needed sets the marginal price for all. Cheap renewables push the price down and shift the curve right.
merit.svg: <line class="ax" x1="40" y1="220" x2="385" y2="220"/><line class="ax" x1="40" y1="220" x2="40" y2="25"/><path d="M385,220 l-7,-4 v8z M40,25 l-4,7 h8z" fill="#8794ab"/><text x="212.5" y="250" text-anchor="middle" class="">Cumulative capacity (MW) →</text><text transform="translate(14,122.5) rotate(-90)" text-anchor="middle">Marginal cost</text><rect class="bx" x="40.0" y="198.0" width="83.8" height="17.0"/><text x="81.875" y="208" text-anchor="middle" class="sm">wind/solar</text><rect class="bx" x="123.8" y="184.4" width="83.8" height="30.6"/><text x="165.625" y="208" text-anchor="middle" class="sm">nuclear</text><rect class="bx" x="207.5" y="155.5" width="67.0" height="59.5"/><text x="241.0" y="208" text-anchor="middle" class="sm">coal</text><rect class="bx" x="274.5" y="121.5" width="60.3" height="93.5"/><text x="304.65000000000003" y="208" text-anchor="middle" class="sm">gas CCGT</text><rect class="bx" x="334.8" y="70.5" width="40.2" height="144.5"/><text x="354.90000000000003" y="208" text-anchor="middle" class="sm">peaker</text><line class="l4 dsh" x1="255" y1="25" x2="255" y2="220"/><text x="255" y="20" text-anchor="middle" class="sm">demand</text><line class="l2 dsh" x1="40" y1="121.49999999999999" x2="255" y2="121.49999999999999"/><text x="330" y="50" text-anchor="middle" class="sm">last plant needed</text><text x="330" y="66" text-anchor="middle" class="sm">sets the price</text>

knee.s: Capacity fades slowly and almost linearly, then accelerates after the knee, often from lithium plating or loss of active material. Operators watch for early knee signs and retire or derate before end of life.

ccv.s: First constant current (CC) until the cell reaches its voltage limit, then constant voltage (CV) while the current tapers off. The CV phase prevents overvoltage at the top of charge.

rc.s: A capacitor charging through a resistor reaches 63% of the supply after one time constant τ = RC, 95% after 3τ, and about 99% after 5τ. Precharge circuits use this to avoid inrush current.

cap.s: During a network partition a distributed store must choose: stay consistent (refuse some requests) or stay available (answer, maybe with stale data). Partitions cannot be ruled out, so the real choice is between C and A.
cap.svg: <polygon class="bx" points="200,30 70,215 330,215"/><text x="200" y="22" text-anchor="middle" class="">Consistency</text><text x="60" y="235" text-anchor="middle" class="">Availability</text><text x="340" y="235" text-anchor="middle" class="">Partition tolerance</text><text x="200" y="150" text-anchor="middle" class="">Pick two</text><text x="200" y="172" text-anchor="middle" class="sm">but partitions happen,</text><text x="200" y="188" text-anchor="middle" class="sm">so choose C or A</text>

rocof.s: After a sudden loss of generation, frequency falls at a rate set by the lost power and the system inertia: RoCoF = ΔP·f₀ / (2·H·S). Low-inertia grids fall faster, leaving less time for reserves, which is a role for fast batteries.

trun.s: Past the onset temperature, exothermic reactions inside the cell release more heat than can be removed, so temperature rises faster and faster. Cooling, early detection, spacing and venting limit propagation to neighbours.

arb.s: Buy and charge in the cheap hours, discharge in the expensive ones. Profit is the spread multiplied by the energy, minus losses from round-trip efficiency and degradation cost.

trafo.s: Two windings share a magnetic core. An alternating current in the primary creates a changing flux that induces a voltage in the secondary, scaled by the turns ratio. It only works on AC, and power in ≈ power out.

acdc.s: Alternating current changes direction periodically, 50 or 60 times per second on the grid. Direct current flows one way at a steady level. Batteries store and deliver DC, so a converter links them to the AC grid.

earth.s: A damaged insulator lets the live conductor touch the metal frame. Because the frame is bonded to ground, a large fault current flows through the protective earth path, tripping the breaker or RCD and keeping the frame from staying at dangerous voltage.
